Pleasant
PLEZ-unt
adj.
From Old French plaisant, from Latin placere, to please. Webster 1828: pleasing; agreeable; grateful to the mind or to the senses. In Scripture it is a two-edged word: the first sin was pleasant to the eyes, and the believer’s inheritance falls in pleasant places.

Biblical Definition

Pleasant is one of Scripture’s most carefully balanced words, because it is used of the bait and of the blessing with equal frankness. The fall turns on it: when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat (Genesis 3:6) — three appeals, of which the middle is bare pleasantness. John’s lust of the eyes is a summary of that clause. Yet Scripture never concludes from this that pleasantness is suspect in itself, because God is the author of it. The believer’s portion is described in exactly the same terms: The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage (Psalm 16:6), a psalm that ends in resurrection and pleasures for evermore. Solomon commends good speech in the same key: Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones (Proverbs 16:24). David’s elegy over Saul and Jonathan calls them lovely and pleasant in their lives (2 Samuel 1:23) — generous language about a king who had hunted him. And the great verse on the unity of brethren stands on it: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! (Psalm 133:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PLEASANT as pleasing, agreeable, grateful to the mind or to the senses; cheerful, enlivening; and, in a lower sense, trifling or merry. The mixture of high and low in his own entry answers to the mixture in Scripture’s usage.

expand to see more

PLEASANT, a. — Pleasing; agreeable; grateful to the mind or to the senses; as a pleasant prospect, a pleasant taste.

Cheerful; enlivening; as pleasant company, a pleasant countenance.

Gay; lively; humorous; sportive; sometimes with the implication of trifling.

Trifling; adapted rather to mirth than to use — a sense Webster marks as inferior and now nearly obsolete.

From Latin placere, to please, whence also placid, complacent, and please itself.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:6 — "And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat."

Psalm 16:6 — "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage."

Psalm 133:1 — "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!"

Proverbs 16:24 — "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones."

2 Samuel 1:23 — "Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided: they were swifter than eagles, they were stronger than lions."

Modern Corruption

Pleasantness has been promoted from a good thing to the governing test of a message, so that a doctrine’s pleasantness is now widely treated as evidence of its truth — the exact reasoning of Genesis 3:6.

expand to see more

Eve saw that the tree was pleasant to the eyes. The narrative records her reasoning in full and does not say she was stupid; she assessed the fruit by appetite, appearance, and promised benefit, which is how every unbeliever assesses every claim. The modern form of it is the assumption that a hard doctrine is thereby probably false — that a God who elects, or who judges, or who has fixed the boundaries of marriage, cannot be the real one because such a God is unpleasant. Isaiah described the market for that precisely: speak unto us smooth things, prophesy deceits. The corrective is not a taste for grim doctrine. It is the recognition that pleasantness is a quality of things, not a test of them, and that the serpent’s whole method was to make the forbidden look better than the given.

The opposite error is a sour Christianity that treats every pleasure as a snare, and Scripture gives it no support at all. Psalm 16, which David wrote and Peter preached at Pentecost as a prophecy of the resurrection, contains the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places and ends with at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore. Psalm 133 calls the unity of brethren pleasant and compares it to the anointing oil running down Aaron’s beard. Proverbs commends pleasant words as honeycomb and health to the bones. A Christian who cannot say of his own portion that the lines have fallen in pleasant places has usually mistaken ingratitude for seriousness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew naim (H5273), pleasant, delightful, from naem (H5276), to be sweet or agreeable — the root behind the name Naomi; and ta’avah, desire, in Genesis 3:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew naim (H5273) — pleasant, delightful, sweet; Psalm 16:6, 133:1, 2 Samuel 1:23.

Hebrew naem (H5276) — to be pleasant, agreeable; the root of Naomi, my pleasantness (Ruth 1:20).

Hebrew ta’avah (H8378) — desire, longing; pleasant to the eyes in Genesis 3:6 renders a related idea of what draws the eye.

Hebrew chemdah (H2532) — desirable, precious; used of the pleasant land in Jeremiah 3:19 and Zechariah 7:14.

Greek hedus — sweet, pleasant; the root of hedone, pleasure, and of philedonos, lovers of pleasure (2 Timothy 3:4).

Usage

"Pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired (Genesis 3:6) — the assessment that lost Eden."

"The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places (Psalm 16:6) — the believer’s estimate of his own portion."

"How good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity (Psalm 133:1) — pleasantness as a mark of the church."
